The Rio Grande. Flowing approximately one thousand nine hundred miles from the San Juan Mountains of Colorado southward through New Mexico and along the border between Texas and Mexico before emptying into the Gulf of Mexico, the Rio Grande is a defining river of the American Southwest and Mexico. It serves as the international boundary between the two countries and a crucial water source in an arid region. The river originates in the San Juan Mountains of southwestern Colorado at elevations exceeding twelve thousand feet, flowing southward into New Mexico and then south-southeastward. Spanish explorers named it Rio Grande, meaning big river or great river. The Rio Grande forms the international boundary between the United States and Mexico for approximately one thousand two hundred fifty miles, from El Paso, Texas, to the Gulf of Mexico. It flows through a series of dramatic canyons in New Mexico, including the Big Bend region in Texas, a popular wilderness destination. The river is heavily dammed and diverted for irrigation throughout its course. By the time it reaches Mexico, much of its water is consumed, leading to ongoing disputes over water allocation between the two nations. The river was named in numerous treaties between the United States and Mexico as the official border, particularly significant after the Mexican-American War from eighteen forty-six to eighteen forty-eight. It supports a unique riparian ecosystem that has been heavily impacted by water diversion and invasive species, while the river's mouth creates a delta in Mexico.
